entry.sum: The probability generating function $G_X(s) = E[s^X] = \sum_k P(X=k)s^k$ of a variable with values in $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, and the moment generating function $M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]$ of any real variable, package a whole distribution into one function. Derivatives at $s = 1$ or $t = 0$ give moments, and for independent variables the generating function of a sum is the product of the generating functions.
entry.why: They turn convolutions into products, which is how one shows that sums of independent Poisson or normal variables stay Poisson or normal, analyses random sums and branching processes, proves the central limit theorem, and obtains exponentially small Chernoff tail bounds.

links.note: A PGF is an ordinary generating function with probabilities as coefficients, so factorising polynomials answers questions such as which pairs of dice give the same distribution of totals.
MGFs identify the sampling distributions of sums and means of independent observations, for example that the sum of independent exponential waiting times has a gamma distribution.
Chernoff bounds, obtained by optimising the MGF in Markov's inequality, are the standard tool for showing that randomised algorithms and hashing schemes succeed with overwhelming probability.

refs: Ross, A First Course in Probability
Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes
Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1

blocks.body:
A random variable is described by a whole list of numbers: the probabilities $P(X = 0), P(X = 1), P(X = 2), \dots$, or a density. Adding independent random variables means convolving such lists, which is clumsy. The trick of this page is to package the whole distribution into a single function. Adding independent variables then becomes multiplying functions, and moments such as the mean and variance fall out by differentiating.

There are two versions. The probability generating function (PGF) is made for variables taking values $0, 1, 2, \dots$ and is exactly an ordinary [[generating-functions|generating function]] whose coefficients are probabilities. The moment generating function (MGF) works for any real random variable and has the moments $E[X^n]$ as its [[taylor|Taylor coefficients]] (up to factorials). Both rest on [[random-variables|expectation]] and on [[power-series]].

blocks.title: Probability and moment generating functions
blocks.body:
Let $X$ take values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ with $p_k = P(X = k)$. Its probability generating function is
$$G_X(s) = E\left[s^X\right] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} p_k s^k .$$
For any real random variable $X$, its moment generating function is
$$M_X(t) = E\left[e^{tX}\right],$$
defined for those real $t$ where the expectation is finite. We say $X$ has an MGF when $M_X(t)$ is finite for all $t$ in some open interval $(-h, h)$ with $h > 0$.

The PGF is a power series with nonnegative coefficients summing to $1$, so it converges at least for $|s| \le 1$ and $G_X(1) = 1$. For such $X$ the two functions are related by $M_X(t) = G_X(e^t)$.

blocks.title: The PGF: a distribution as a polynomial
blocks.body:
Take a fair six-sided die. Its PGF is
$$G(s) = \tfrac16\left(s + s^2 + s^3 + s^4 + s^5 + s^6\right).$$
Nothing has been lost: the coefficient of $s^k$ is $P(X = k)$, and in general $p_k = G^{(k)}(0)/k!$, so the PGF determines the distribution.

Now differentiate. Since $G'(s) = \sum k p_k s^{k-1}$, setting $s = 1$ gives $G'(1) = \sum k p_k = E[X]$. Differentiating again, $G''(1) = \sum k(k-1)p_k = E[X(X-1)]$, the second factorial moment. Hence
$$E[X] = G'(1), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X) = G''(1) + G'(1) - G'(1)^2 .$$
For the die, $G'(1) = 21/6 = 7/2$ and $G''(1) = 70/6 = 35/3$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 35/3 + 7/2 - 49/4 = 35/12$. (When $X$ has infinite mean, $G'(s) \to \infty$ as $s \to 1^-$; the formulas are read as limits from the left.)

The main reason to use a PGF is sums. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then so are $s^X$ and $s^Y$, and the expectation of a product of independent variables is the product of the expectations:
$$G_{X+Y}(s) = E\left[s^X s^Y\right] = E\left[s^X\right] E\left[s^Y\right] = G_X(s)\,G_Y(s).$$
Multiplying the polynomials automatically performs the convolution $P(X + Y = n) = \sum_k P(X = k)P(Y = n-k)$.

Some standard PGFs, with $q = 1 - p$:

- Bernoulli($p$): $q + ps$. So Binomial($n, p$), a sum of $n$ independent Bernoullis, has $G(s) = (q + ps)^n$.
- Poisson($\lambda$): $\sum e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k s^k/k! = e^{\lambda(s-1)}$.
- Geometric($p$) on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ (the number of trials up to and including the first success): $G(s) = \dfrac{ps}{1 - qs}$ for $|s| < 1/q$.

From $(q + ps)^n$ we get $G'(1) = np$ and $G''(1) = n(n-1)p^2$, so the variance is $n(n-1)p^2 + np - n^2p^2 = np(1-p)$, with no binomial-coefficient juggling at all.

blocks.title: The MGF: moments as Taylor coefficients
blocks.body:
For a variable with a density, or one taking negative or non-integer values, $s^X$ is awkward, so we write $s = e^t$ and use $M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]$. Expanding the exponential,
$$M_X(t) = E\left[\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{t^n X^n}{n!}\right] = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{E[X^n]}{n!}\, t^n ,$$
and when $M_X$ is finite on an interval $(-h, h)$ this exchange of sum and expectation is justified, $M_X$ is a convergent power series there, and
$$M_X^{(n)}(0) = E\left[X^n\right].$$
That is the origin of the name: the MGF generates the moments.

Two examples worth knowing. If $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$, then $M_X(t) = \int_0^\infty e^{tx}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,dx = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}$ for $t < \lambda$ (and $M_X(t) = \infty$ for $t \ge \lambda$). Expanding $1/(1 - t/\lambda) = \sum t^n/\lambda^n$ shows at once that $E[X^n] = n!/\lambda^n$. If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, completing the square in the integral gives $M_X(t) = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$ for all $t$.

Two rules do most of the work: $M_{aX + b}(t) = e^{bt} M_X(at)$, and $M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y$ when $X, Y$ are independent (same proof as for PGFs). For example, if $X \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)$ and $Y \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)$ are independent, the product of their MGFs is $e^{(\mu_1 + \mu_2)t + (\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)t^2/2}$, the MGF of $N(\mu_1 + \mu_2, \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)$. To conclude that $X + Y$ really has that distribution we need the next theorem.

blocks.title: Uniqueness and the product rule
blocks.body:
1. (PGFs) If $G_X(s) = G_Y(s)$ for all $s$ in some interval $[0, \varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon > 0$, then $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution.
2. (MGFs) If $M_X(t)$ and $M_Y(t)$ are both finite and equal for all $t$ in an open interval $(-h, h)$, $h > 0$, then $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution.
3. (Sums) If $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are independent, then $G_{X_1 + \cdots + X_n} = \prod G_{X_i}$ and $M_{X_1 + \cdots + X_n} = \prod M_{X_i}$ wherever the factors are finite.

blocks.title: Proof of parts 1 and 3
blocks.body:
Part 1: $G_X$ and $G_Y$ are power series converging on $(-1, 1)$, and two power series that agree on $[0, \varepsilon)$ have the same coefficients, because the $k$th coefficient equals $G^{(k)}(0)/k!$ and the derivatives at $0$ can be computed using only values on $[0, \varepsilon)$ (one-sided limits of difference quotients). So $P(X = k) = P(Y = k)$ for every $k$.

Part 3: the variables $s^{X_i}$ (or $e^{tX_i}$) are independent and nonnegative, and for independent nonnegative variables $E[\prod Z_i] = \prod E[Z_i]$, so the expectation of the product of $s^{X_i}$ factorises.

Part 2 is genuinely deeper: it is an inversion theorem for the Laplace transform, or, extending $t$ to complex values, for the Fourier transform (the characteristic function). We use it without proof; see the references.

blocks.title: Random sums: composition of PGFs
blocks.body:
A common model: a random number $N$ of customers arrive, and customer $i$ spends $X_i$, with the $X_i$ independent, identically distributed and independent of $N$. The total $S = X_1 + \cdots + X_N$ (with $S = 0$ if $N = 0$) is a random sum. Conditioning on $N$,
$$G_S(s) = E\left[E\left[s^S \mid N\right]\right] = E\left[G_X(s)^N\right] = G_N\big(G_X(s)\big).$$
So the PGF of a random sum is a composition. Differentiating with the chain rule at $s = 1$ (where $G_X(1) = 1$) gives $E[S] = G_N'(1)\,G_X'(1) = E[N]\,E[X]$, which is intuitive; the variance formula $\operatorname{Var}(S) = E[N]\operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(N)E[X]^2$ follows from the second derivative. The same composition rule drives branching processes: if each individual has offspring with PGF $G$, the size of generation $n$ has PGF $G \circ G \circ \cdots \circ G$ ($n$ times).

blocks.title: Tail bounds and the characteristic function
blocks.body:
MGFs also give tail bounds. For any $t > 0$, the event $X \ge a$ is the event $e^{tX} \ge e^{ta}$, so Markov's inequality gives
$$P(X \ge a) \le e^{-ta} M_X(t), \qquad \text{hence} \qquad P(X \ge a) \le \inf_{t > 0} e^{-ta} M_X(t).$$
This is the Chernoff bound. For $X \sim \text{Binomial}(100, 1/2)$ and $a = 75$, minimising $e^{-75t}\left(\frac{1 + e^t}{2}\right)^{100}$ gives $e^t = 3$ and the bound $\approx 2.1 \times 10^{-6}$; the true probability is about $2.8 \times 10^{-7}$. Chebyshev's inequality would only give a bound of about $0.04$ for this event, so the exponential bound is enormously better. The bound equals $e^{-100D}$ with $D = \tfrac34 \ln \tfrac32 + \tfrac14 \ln \tfrac12 \approx 0.131$, the relative [[entropy]] (in nats) of a coin with bias $3/4$ from a fair coin.

The MGF has one weakness: it may not exist. For the Cauchy distribution, or any distribution with a heavy tail such as a density proportional to $1/x^3$ for large $x$, $E[e^{tX}] = \infty$ for every $t > 0$. The fix is the characteristic function $\varphi_X(t) = E[e^{itX}]$, which is finite for every random variable because $|e^{itX}| = 1$. It has the same product rule and uniqueness property, and Lévy's continuity theorem (stated here without proof) says that if $\varphi_{X_n}(t) \to \varphi_X(t)$ for every $t$ then $X_n \to X$ in distribution. When MGFs exist on a common interval around $0$, the analogous statement for MGFs also holds (again without proof here), and this is the standard route to the central limit theorem in [[limit-theorems]].
Use PGFs to find the distribution of the total $T$ of two fair dice, then its mean and variance.
blocks.solution:
By the product rule, $G_T(s) = G(s)^2 = \frac{1}{36}\left(s + \cdots + s^6\right)^2$. Expanding,
$$G_T(s) = \tfrac{1}{36}\left(s^2 + 2s^3 + 3s^4 + 4s^5 + 5s^6 + 6s^7 + 5s^8 + 4s^9 + 3s^{10} + 2s^{11} + s^{12}\right),$$
so for instance $P(T = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6$.

For the moments, differentiate $G_T = G^2$: $G_T' = 2GG'$, so $G_T'(1) = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot \tfrac72 = 7$. Then $G_T'' = 2(G')^2 + 2GG''$, so $G_T''(1) = 2 \cdot \tfrac{49}{4} + 2 \cdot \tfrac{35}{3} = \tfrac{287}{6}$. Hence
$$\operatorname{Var}(T) = \tfrac{287}{6} + 7 - 49 = \tfrac{35}{6},$$
twice the variance $35/12$ of one die, as it must be for independent summands.

blocks.body: A hen lays $N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ eggs, and each egg independently hatches with probability $p$. Find the distribution of the number $H$ of chicks.
blocks.solution:
$H$ is a random sum of $N$ independent Bernoulli($p$) variables, independent of $N$, so
$$G_H(s) = G_N\big(G_X(s)\big) = e^{\lambda\left((q + ps) - 1\right)} = e^{\lambda p (s - 1)} .$$
This is the PGF of Poisson($\lambda p$), so by uniqueness $H \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda p)$. Thinning a Poisson count keeps it Poisson.

blocks.body: Can two six-sided dice be loaded (each face of each die given some probability, the two dice rolled independently) so that the total is equally likely to be each of $2, 3, \dots, 12$?
blocks.solution:
No. Suppose die A shows $k$ with probability $a_k$ and die B with probability $b_k$. The total would have to have PGF
$$G_A(s)G_B(s) = \tfrac{1}{11}\left(s^2 + s^3 + \cdots + s^{12}\right).$$
Comparing the coefficients of $s^2$ and $s^{12}$, $a_1 b_1 = a_6 b_6 = 1/11$, so $a_1, a_6, b_1, b_6$ are all positive. Write $G_A(s) = s\,A(s)$ with $A(s) = a_1 + a_2 s + \cdots + a_6 s^5$, and similarly $G_B(s) = s\,B(s)$. Since $a_6 > 0$, $A$ is a real polynomial of odd degree $5$, so it has a real root $r$; then
$$A(r)B(r) = \tfrac{1}{11}\left(1 + r + \cdots + r^{10}\right) = 0.$$
But $1 + r + \cdots + r^{10}$ has no real root: at $r = 1$ it equals $11$, and for $r \ne 1$ it equals $(r^{11} - 1)/(r - 1)$, which vanishes only if $r^{11} = 1$, impossible for real $r \ne 1$. Contradiction.

The same factorisation idea shows what is possible. The "Sicherman dice" with faces $1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4$ and $1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8$ satisfy
$$\left(s + 2s^2 + 2s^3 + s^4\right)\left(s + s^3 + s^4 + s^5 + s^6 + s^8\right) = \left(s + s^2 + \cdots + s^6\right)^2,$$
so they give exactly the same distribution of totals as two ordinary dice; they come from regrouping the irreducible factors $s$, $1 + s$, $1 + s + s^2$, $1 - s + s^2$ of $s + \cdots + s^6$.

blocks.body:
- The PGF is only for variables with values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$. For other variables use the MGF or the characteristic function.
- Uniqueness of MGFs needs $M_X$ finite on an open interval around $0$. A function finite only at $t = 0$ (Cauchy, or any heavy-tailed law) tells you nothing.
- Knowing all the moments $E[X^n]$ does not, in general, determine a distribution: the lognormal distribution has the same moments as other, different distributions, and its MGF is infinite for every $t > 0$. Moments determine the law when the MGF exists near $0$.
- $M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y$ needs independence (uncorrelated is not enough). For $Y = X$ we get $M_{2X}(t) = M_X(2t)$, not $M_X(t)^2$.
- In the random-sum formula $G_N(G_X(s))$ the order matters, and $N$ must be independent of the $X_i$.

The PGF is the probabilistic face of [[generating-functions]]: counting problems often become probability problems by normalising coefficients, and vice versa. The MGF is a two-sided Laplace transform (compare [[laplace-transform]]), and the characteristic function is a [[fourier-transform]] of the distribution; the product rule for sums is the convolution theorem. MGFs and characteristic functions give the cleanest proofs in [[limit-theorems]], Chernoff bounds are a workhorse of the [[probabilistic-method]], and the logarithm $\ln M_X(t)$ (the cumulant generating function) is the bridge to large deviations and to [[entropy]]. In [[markov-chains]] and branching processes, iterated PGFs compute extinction probabilities.

1. A fair tetrahedral die has faces $1, 2, 3, 4$. Write down its PGF and use it to find the probability that the total of three such dice is $6$.
2. A random variable has MGF $M(t) = (1 - 2t)^{-3}$ for $t < 1/2$. Find its mean and variance.
3. Show that the sum of $n$ independent Geometric($p$) variables on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ has PGF $\left(\dfrac{ps}{1 - qs}\right)^n$, and deduce its mean.
4. If $N \sim \text{Geometric}(p)$ on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ and the $X_i$ are independent Poisson($\mu$), independent of $N$, find $E[S]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ for $S = X_1 + \cdots + X_N$.

entry.sum: Monte Carlo methods estimate a number by writing it as an expectation $\theta = E[f(X)]$, simulating many independent copies of $X$, and averaging. The law of large numbers makes the average converge to $\theta$, and the central limit theorem says the error is about $\sigma/\sqrt n$ after $n$ samples, whatever the dimension of the problem.
entry.why: Simulation is often the only practical way to compute high-dimensional integrals, probabilities in complicated models, and expected behaviour of queues, networks, portfolios and physical systems; the same ideas underlie randomised algorithms and Markov chain Monte Carlo.

links.note: Monte Carlo integration has error of order $n^{-1/2}$ independent of dimension, which makes it the method of choice for integrals over spaces of many dimensions where grid-based quadrature is infeasible.
Bayesian posterior distributions are explored by Markov chain Monte Carlo, and bootstrap confidence intervals are computed by resampling simulations.
The Metropolis algorithm was introduced to sample configurations of particle systems in statistical mechanics, and Monte Carlo transport simulations track neutrons and photons through matter.

refs: Ross, A First Course in Probability
Robert & Casella, Monte Carlo Statistical Methods

blocks.body:
What is the probability that a random hand of thirteen cards contains a void suit? What is the volume of a complicated region in ten-dimensional space? How long, on average, does a queue at a bank take to clear? Some of these questions have exact answers that are painful to derive, and some have none at all. Monte Carlo methods answer all of them the same way: make the computer play the random experiment many times and average what happens.

This page explains why that works (the [[limit-theorems|law of large numbers]]), how accurate it is (an error of order $1/\sqrt{n}$ after $n$ runs, by the central limit theorem), how to simulate a prescribed distribution, and how to improve accuracy without running longer.

blocks.title: Estimating by averaging
blocks.body:
Drop $n$ points uniformly at random in the square $[0,1]^2$ and count how many land inside the quarter disc $x^2 + y^2 \le 1$. Each point lands there with probability $p = \pi/4$, so the fraction of hits is close to $\pi/4$ and four times it is close to $\pi$. That is the whole idea: write the number you want as an expectation, simulate the random variable, and average.

More generally, suppose we want $\theta = E[f(X)]$ for some random variable $X$ we can simulate and some function $f$. Any integral can be put in this form; for instance
$$\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx = E[g(U)], \qquad U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1),$$
and a probability is the expectation of an indicator: $P(A) = E[\mathbf{1}_A]$. Draw independent copies $X_1, \dots, X_n$ and form the sample mean. The law of large numbers guarantees that this converges to $\theta$, and the central limit theorem tells us how fast.

The striking feature is that the error does not depend on dimension. If $X$ is uniform on $[0,1]^{10}$, the error is still of order $\sigma/\sqrt n$, where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of $f(X)$. A grid-based method with $m$ points per axis needs $m^{10}$ function evaluations, so in high dimensions Monte Carlo usually wins, even though in one dimension it is far slower than the methods in [[interpolation-quadrature]].

blocks.title: Monte Carlo estimator
blocks.body:
Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent with the same distribution as $X$, and suppose $\theta = E[f(X)]$ and $\sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var}(f(X)) < \infty$. The crude Monte Carlo estimator of $\theta$ is
$$\hat\theta_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i),$$
and its standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, estimated in practice by $s/\sqrt n$ where $s$ is the sample standard deviation of the values $f(X_i)$.

The standard error is the typical size of $\hat\theta_n - \theta$; it is the number to report with every simulation result.

blocks.title: Accuracy of crude Monte Carlo
blocks.body:
With the notation above:
1. $E[\hat\theta_n] = \theta$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n) = \sigma^2/n$.
2. $\hat\theta_n \to \theta$ with probability $1$ as $n \to \infty$.
3. If $\sigma > 0$, then $\sqrt n\,(\hat\theta_n - \theta)/\sigma$ converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$, so for large $n$ the interval $\hat\theta_n \pm 1.96\,s/\sqrt n$ contains $\theta$ with probability close to $95\%$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: Part 1 is linearity of expectation together with the fact that variances of independent variables add: $\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum f(X_i)\right) = n\sigma^2$, and dividing by $n$ divides the variance by $n^2$. Part 2 is the strong law of large numbers and part 3 is the central limit theorem, both from [[limit-theorems]], applied to the independent, identically distributed variables $f(X_i)$. Replacing $\sigma$ by $s$ in part 3 is justified because $s \to \sigma$ with probability $1$ by the strong law, and Slutsky's theorem (a standard result, not proved here) lets us substitute a consistent estimate.

blocks.title: A run, with its error bar
blocks.body:
Here is a real run. Using NumPy's generator default_rng with seed $2026$, we drew $10{,}000$ uniform numbers $U_i$ and averaged $e^{U_i}$ to estimate $\int_0^1 e^x\,dx = e - 1 \approx 1.71828$. The run gave
$$\hat\theta = 1.72725, \qquad s = 0.49325, \qquad s/\sqrt n = 0.00493,$$
so the $95\%$ interval is $1.72725 \pm 0.00967$, that is $[1.71758,\ 1.73692]$, which does contain $e - 1$. Another seed gives other numbers, but the standard error is always close to the theoretical $\sqrt{0.24204/10{,}000} \approx 0.00492$. To gain one more correct decimal digit we would need $100$ times as many samples. This square-root law is the price of Monte Carlo, and the rest of the page is largely about lowering $\sigma$ instead of raising $n$.

blocks.title: Turning uniforms into other distributions
blocks.body:
A computer produces pseudo-random numbers: a deterministic recurrence whose output passes statistical tests for independent Uniform$(0,1)$ variables. Everything else is built from these.

Discrete variables are easy. To simulate $X$ with $P(X = x_j) = p_j$, draw $U$ and return $x_j$ when $p_1 + \cdots + p_{j-1} \le U < p_1 + \cdots + p_j$; the interval has length $p_j$. The continuous version of this idea is the next theorem.

blocks.title: Inverse transform method
blocks.body: Let $F$ be a distribution function and define $F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}$ for $0 < u < 1$. If $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$, then $X = F^{-1}(U)$ has distribution function $F$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: Because $F$ is non-decreasing and right-continuous, the set $\{x : F(x) \ge u\}$ is an interval $[F^{-1}(u), \infty)$ that contains its left endpoint. Hence $F^{-1}(u) \le x$ if and only if $u \le F(x)$. Therefore $P(X \le x) = P(U \le F(x)) = F(x)$.

blocks.title: Two workhorses: inversion and rejection
blocks.body:
For the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$, $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$, so $F^{-1}(u) = -\ln(1-u)/\lambda$. Since $1 - U$ is again uniform, $X = -\ln(U)/\lambda$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$.

When $F^{-1}$ has no usable formula, rejection sampling often helps. Suppose we want density $f$, we can sample from a density $g$, and $f(x) \le c\,g(x)$ for all $x$. Repeat: draw $Y$ from $g$ and an independent uniform $U$; if $U \le f(Y)/(c\,g(Y))$, accept and output $Y$; otherwise try again. Each attempt succeeds with probability $1/c$, the output has density exactly $f$, and the number of attempts is geometric with mean $c$.

The proof is one line: for one attempt,
$$P(Y \le x \text{ and accept}) = \int_{-\infty}^x g(y)\,\frac{f(y)}{c\,g(y)}\,dy = \frac{F(x)}{c},$$
and letting $x \to \infty$ gives $P(\text{accept}) = 1/c$. Dividing, the accepted value has distribution function $F$; since attempts are independent, the same holds for the first accepted value.

blocks.title: Variance reduction
blocks.body:
Since the error is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, any change that keeps the mean $\theta$ but lowers $\sigma$ is as good as more samples. Three standard tricks, illustrated on $\theta = E[e^U] = e - 1$, where crude Monte Carlo has $\operatorname{Var}(e^U) = \frac{e^2 - 1}{2} - (e - 1)^2 \approx 0.24204$:

1. Antithetic variables. Use $U$ and $1 - U$ together: $\tfrac12\left(e^U + e^{1-U}\right)$ still has mean $\theta$. Because $e^x$ is increasing, $e^U$ and $e^{1-U}$ are negatively correlated, and the variance of the pair average is about $0.003912$, compared with $0.12102$ for the average of two independent draws. That is a reduction by a factor of about $31$ for the same number of function evaluations.
2. Control variates. If $Y$ is simulated alongside $f(X)$ and $E[Y] = \mu$ is known, use $f(X) + c(Y - \mu)$. Its variance $\operatorname{Var}f(X) + 2c\operatorname{Cov}(f(X), Y) + c^2\operatorname{Var}Y$ is smallest at $c^* = -\operatorname{Cov}(f(X), Y)/\operatorname{Var}Y$, where it equals $(1 - \rho^2)\operatorname{Var}f(X)$, with $\rho$ the correlation. With $Y = U$: $\operatorname{Cov}(e^U, U) = (3 - e)/2$, so $c^* = -6(3 - e) \approx -1.690$ and the variance drops to about $0.00394$.
3. Importance sampling. Write $E_f[h(X)] = E_g\left[h(Y)\,f(Y)/g(Y)\right]$ with $Y$ drawn from a different density $g$ that puts more mass where $h f$ is large. The ratio $f/g$ is the importance weight. It is essential for rare events, as Example 3 shows.

Re-running the seed-$2026$ experiment antithetically with $5000$ pairs (so again $10{,}000$ evaluations of $e^x$) gave $1.71702$ with standard error $0.00088$, an error bar more than five times narrower.
How many points are needed in the quarter-disc experiment to estimate $\pi$ with a standard error of at most $0.001$?
blocks.solution:
Each point gives $Z = 4\cdot\mathbf 1\{\text{hit}\}$, a variable with mean $\pi$ and variance $16p(1-p)$ where $p = \pi/4$, so
$$\operatorname{Var}(Z) = 16\cdot\frac\pi4\left(1 - \frac\pi4\right) = \pi(4 - \pi) \approx 2.6968.$$
The standard error after $n$ points is $\sqrt{2.6968/n}$, and this is at most $0.001$ when $n \ge 2.6968 \times 10^6$. So about $2.7$ million points buy three decimal places of $\pi$, which shows how slowly crude Monte Carlo converges.

blocks.body: Simulate from the density $f(x) = 6x(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ by rejection from the uniform distribution. What is the acceptance probability, and why not use inversion?
blocks.solution:
Take $g(x) = 1$ on $[0,1]$. The maximum of $f$ is at $x = 1/2$, where $f = 3/2$, so the smallest valid constant is $c = 3/2$. Draw $Y, U$ uniform and accept $Y$ if $U \le f(Y)/c = 4Y(1 - Y)$. Each attempt is accepted with probability $1/c = 2/3$, and on average $3/2$ attempts are needed per sample.

Inversion would require solving $F(x) = 3x^2 - 2x^3 = u$, a cubic, for every sample. Rejection needs only a multiplication and a comparison.

blocks.body: Estimate $p = P(Z > 4)$ for $Z \sim N(0,1)$. Compare crude Monte Carlo with importance sampling from $N(4,1)$.
blocks.solution:
The true value is $p \approx 3.167 \times 10^{-5}$. Crude Monte Carlo averages the indicator $\mathbf 1\{Z > 4\}$, whose standard deviation is $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$; the relative standard error of one draw is $\sqrt{p(1-p)}/p \approx 177.7$. With a million draws we would see only about $32$ hits.

Now draw $Y \sim N(4, 1)$, whose density is $\varphi(y - 4)$ where $\varphi$ is the standard normal density. The weight is
$$w(y) = \frac{\varphi(y)}{\varphi(y - 4)} = e^{-4y + 8},$$
and the estimator averages $\mathbf 1\{Y > 4\}\,w(Y)$, which has mean $p$. Its second moment is
$$\int_4^\infty \frac{\varphi(y)^2}{\varphi(y-4)}\,dy = e^{8}\int_4^\infty \varphi(y)e^{-4y}\,dy = e^{16}\,P(Z > 8) \approx 5.528 \times 10^{-9},$$
using $\varphi(y)e^{-4y} = e^{8}\varphi(y + 4)$. Subtracting $p^2$, the variance is about $4.525 \times 10^{-9}$, and the relative standard error of one draw is about $2.12$. Since the number of samples needed for a given accuracy scales with the variance, importance sampling needs about $7000$ times fewer samples here.

blocks.body: Buffon's needle. A floor has parallel lines a distance $d$ apart, and a needle of length $\ell \le d$ is dropped at random. Show that it crosses a line with probability $2\ell/(\pi d)$, and explain how this gives a (slow) physical Monte Carlo estimate of $\pi$.
blocks.solution:
Describe the needle by the distance $y$ from its midpoint to the nearest line and the acute angle $\theta$ it makes with the lines. "At random" means $y$ is uniform on $[0, d/2]$ and $\theta$ is uniform on $[0, \pi/2]$, independently. The needle reaches the nearest line exactly when $y \le \frac{\ell}{2}\sin\theta$ (the condition $\ell \le d$ ensures it can cross at most one line). The pair $(y, \theta)$ is uniform on a rectangle of area $\frac d2\cdot\frac\pi2$, so
$$P(\text{cross}) = \frac{4}{\pi d}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\ell}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta = \frac{4}{\pi d}\cdot\frac{\ell}{2} = \frac{2\ell}{\pi d}.$$
If $H$ of $n$ needles cross, then $H/n \approx 2\ell/(\pi d)$, so $\pi \approx 2\ell n/(dH)$. This is a Monte Carlo estimate of $\pi$ in which the random number generator is the act of throwing needles.

blocks.body:
- Reporting an estimate without its standard error. A simulation answer is a number with an error bar.
- Expecting fast convergence. Halving the error costs four times as many samples.
- Infinite variance. If $E[f(X)^2] = \infty$ the law of large numbers may still hold, but the error bars are meaningless and the estimate can jump suddenly. Importance sampling with a proposal $g$ whose tails are lighter than those of $f$ is a common way to create this problem.
- In rejection sampling, $c$ must satisfy $f \le c g$ everywhere; a $c$ that is too small silently produces the wrong distribution.
- Reusing the same random numbers by accident, for instance restarting a generator with the same seed in parallel runs, destroys independence.

The justification rests entirely on [[limit-theorems]] applied to [[random-variables]], and the error bars are the [[confidence-intervals]] of statistics. When independent samples from a distribution are unavailable, Markov chain Monte Carlo builds a [[markov-chains|Markov chain]] whose long-run distribution is the target and averages along its path; this is how Bayesian statisticians and physicists sample from complicated distributions. Simulating random walks and [[brownian-motion]] paths is the standard way to price financial options and to solve [[heat-equation|heat-type equations]] probabilistically. In combinatorics, the [[probabilistic-method]] proves existence by showing that a random construction succeeds with positive probability, and randomised algorithms turn that into a computation.

entry.sum: The entropy $H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)$ of a discrete random variable is its average surprise, measured in bits. It lies between $0$ (no uncertainty) and $\log_2 n$ (uniform on $n$ values), and it is exactly the average number of bits per symbol needed to encode outcomes of $X$ in the long run.
entry.why: Entropy is the limit of lossless data compression, the exponent in large-deviation bounds, the quantity minimised by maximum likelihood and cross-entropy training, and the statistical form of thermodynamic entropy.

links.note: Maximum likelihood estimation is equivalent to minimising the relative entropy from the empirical distribution to the model, and likelihood-ratio tests are built on the same quantity.
Entropy gives sharp counting bounds such as $\binom{n}{k} \le 2^{n h(k/n)}$, and Shearer-type entropy inequalities bound the number of objects whose projections are controlled.
Classifiers and language models are trained by minimising cross-entropy, which equals entropy plus the relative entropy between the data and the model.

refs: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
Ross, A First Course in Probability
MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms

blocks.body:
A friend picks a whole number from $1$ to $16$ and you may ask yes/no questions. Four questions always suffice (halve the range each time), and no strategy can guarantee fewer, because $3$ answers distinguish only $2^3 = 8$ cases. Now suppose the friend picks $1$ half of the time and spreads the other half evenly over the rest. Then it pays to ask "is it $1$?" first, and the average number of questions drops below four. How far can it drop?

Shannon's answer, from 1948, is a single number computed from the probabilities: the entropy. It measures how uncertain a random outcome is, or equivalently how much information you gain on learning it. The same quantity sets the limit for data compression, underlies the measure of difference between distributions used in statistics and machine learning, and is, up to a constant, the entropy of thermodynamics.

blocks.title: Surprise and its average
blocks.body:
If an event has probability $p$, call $\log_2(1/p)$ its surprise. A fair coin landing heads has surprise $1$; an event of probability $1/1024$ has surprise $10$. Surprise is $0$ for a certain event, grows as the event becomes rarer, and adds up for independent events, because $\log(1/(pq)) = \log(1/p) + \log(1/q)$. Up to the choice of base, these properties force the formula $\log(1/p)$ (a functional-equation argument we do not give here).

The entropy of a random variable is its average surprise. For a coin that lands heads with probability $p$ it is
$$h(p) = p\log_2\frac1p + (1-p)\log_2\frac{1}{1-p}.$$
A few values:

- $p = 0.5$: $h = 1$ bit.
- $p = 0.75$ or $0.25$: $h \approx 0.811$.
- $p = 0.9$ or $0.1$: $h \approx 0.469$.
- $p = 0.99$: $h \approx 0.081$.

A very biased coin carries little information per toss, which is why a long record of its tosses can be compressed so well: mostly it says "heads again". The function $h$ is symmetric about $1/2$, concave, and maximal at $p = 1/2$.

blocks.title: Entropy
blocks.body:
Let $X$ take finitely or countably many values with probabilities $p(x) = P(X = x)$. Its entropy is
$$H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x) = E\left[\log_2\frac{1}{p(X)}\right],$$
with the convention $0\log 0 = 0$. With $\log_2$ the unit is the bit; with the natural logarithm it is the nat, and $1$ nat $= \log_2 e \approx 1.443$ bits.

$H(X)$ depends only on the list of probabilities, not on the values $X$ takes: relabelling outcomes does not change it.

blocks.title: Range of entropy
blocks.body:
If $X$ takes at most $n$ values, then
$$0 \le H(X) \le \log_2 n.$$
$H(X) = 0$ exactly when $X$ is constant, and $H(X) = \log_2 n$ exactly when $X$ is uniform on $n$ values.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Each term $p\log_2(1/p)$ is $\ge 0$ for $0 \le p \le 1$, and is $0$ only for $p \in \{0, 1\}$; so $H \ge 0$ with equality only when one value has probability $1$.

For the upper bound, $\log_2$ is strictly concave, so by Jensen's inequality ([[convexity]])
$$H(X) = E\left[\log_2\frac{1}{p(X)}\right] \le \log_2 E\left[\frac{1}{p(X)}\right] = \log_2\sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x)\cdot\frac{1}{p(x)} = \log_2 m,$$
where $m \le n$ is the number of values of positive probability. Equality in Jensen for a strictly concave function needs $1/p(X)$ to be constant, that is, $X$ uniform on its $m$ values, and $\log_2 m = \log_2 n$ needs $m = n$.

blocks.title: Several variables: the chain rule
blocks.body:
For a pair $(X, Y)$, the joint entropy $H(X, Y)$ is the entropy of the pair viewed as one random variable. The conditional entropy
$$H(Y \mid X) = \sum_x p(x)\,H(Y \mid X = x)$$
is the uncertainty left in $Y$ once $X$ is known, averaged over $x$. Since $p(x, y) = p(x)p(y \mid x)$, taking $-\log_2$ and averaging gives the chain rule
$$H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X):$$
learning the pair is learning $X$ and then learning $Y$ given $X$. If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $H(Y \mid X) = H(Y)$ and entropies simply add. In general they are subadditive, $H(X, Y) \le H(X) + H(Y)$, and the gap
$$I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$$
is the mutual information, the amount $X$ tells you about $Y$. The proof that $I \ge 0$ comes from the most useful inequality in the subject.

blocks.title: Relative entropy
blocks.body:
For probability distributions $p$ and $q$ on the same countable set, the relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence) of $p$ from $q$ is
$$D(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)},$$
summed over $x$ with $p(x) > 0$, and set to $+\infty$ if $q(x) = 0$ for some such $x$.

It measures the cost of believing the distribution is $q$ when it is really $p$. It is not symmetric, and it is not a distance in the sense of [[metric-spaces]].

blocks.title: Gibbs' inequality
blocks.body: $D(p \,\|\, q) \ge 0$, with equality if and only if $p = q$. Consequently $I(X; Y) \ge 0$, so (for variables of finite entropy) $H(X, Y) \le H(X) + H(Y)$ and $H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y)$, with equality if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Assume $D < \infty$, and let $S$ be the set where $p > 0$. By Jensen's inequality for the concave $\log_2$, applied to the variable $q(X)/p(X)$ with $X \sim p$,
$$-D(p\,\|\,q) = \sum_{x \in S} p(x)\log_2\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} \le \log_2\sum_{x \in S} p(x)\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} = \log_2\sum_{x \in S} q(x) \le \log_2 1 = 0.$$
Equality needs $q(x)/p(x)$ constant on $S$ (strict concavity) and $\sum_S q = 1$; together these force $q = p$.

For the consequence, a short calculation with $p(x, y) = p(x)p(y \mid x)$ shows that $I(X; Y) = D\big(p_{XY} \,\|\, p_X\,p_Y\big)$, the relative entropy of the joint distribution from the product of the marginals. It is $0$ exactly when $p_{XY} = p_X p_Y$, which is independence.

blocks.title: Entropy as the limit of compression
blocks.body:
A binary code assigns each outcome $x$ a string of bits $c(x)$ of length $\ell(x)$. It is a prefix code if no codeword is the beginning of another, so a stream of codewords can be decoded on the fly. The question from the introduction is a special case: a questioning strategy is a prefix code, the codeword being the sequence of answers.

Kraft's inequality, which we state with only a sketch of the reason, says that prefix codes with lengths $\ell(x)$ exist if and only if $\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1$. (Picture an infinite binary tree: a codeword of length $\ell$ claims a subtree carrying a $2^{-\ell}$ share of the leaves at great depth, and prefix-freeness says these subtrees are disjoint.) Combining this with Gibbs' inequality gives the source coding theorem.

blocks.title: Source coding theorem
blocks.body: For any prefix code for $X$, the expected length satisfies $E[\ell(X)] \ge H(X)$. Conversely, there is a prefix code with $E[\ell(X)] < H(X) + 1$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $K = \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1$ and define the distribution $q(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)}/K$. Then
$$E[\ell(X)] - H(X) = \sum_x p(x)\left(\log_2\frac{1}{2^{-\ell(x)}} - \log_2\frac{1}{p(x)}\right) = \sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{K q(x)} = D(p\,\|\,q) + \log_2\frac1K \ge 0.$$
For the converse, take $\ell(x) = \lceil\log_2(1/p(x))\rceil$. Then $2^{-\ell(x)} \le p(x)$, so Kraft's inequality holds and a prefix code with these lengths exists; and $\ell(x) < \log_2(1/p(x)) + 1$, so averaging gives $E[\ell(X)] < H(X) + 1$.

blocks.title: Long messages and physics
blocks.body:
Coding long blocks of independent outcomes together removes the extra $+1$: $n$ independent copies have entropy $nH$, so the best code spends between $nH$ and $nH + 1$ bits per block, that is, $H + 1/n$ bits per symbol. Entropy is exactly the number of bits per symbol needed in the long run.

The physical story is parallel. Boltzmann's entropy of a system with $W$ equally likely microscopic states is $S = k_B\ln W$, which is $k_B$ times the Shannon entropy in nats of the uniform distribution on those states. When the states are not equally likely, Gibbs' formula $S = -k_B\sum p_i\ln p_i$ is Shannon's formula with a different unit. The principle of maximum entropy says that, among all distributions satisfying given constraints, one should choose the one of largest entropy; with a constraint on the mean energy this produces the Boltzmann distribution $p_i \propto e^{-\beta E_i}$.

Find an optimal prefix code for $X$ with probabilities $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18$, and then for $Y$ with probabilities $0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1$. Compare each expected length with the entropy.
blocks.solution:
For $X$, the codewords $0, 10, 110, 111$ have lengths $\log_2(1/p)$ exactly, so
$$E[\ell] = \tfrac12\cdot1 + \tfrac14\cdot2 + \tfrac18\cdot3 + \tfrac18\cdot3 = 1.75 = H(X).$$
The lower bound is achieved, as it must be when every probability is a power of $\tfrac12$.

For $Y$, Huffman's algorithm repeatedly merges the two least likely items: $0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3$, then $0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6$, then $0.6 + 0.4 = 1$. Reading off the depths gives lengths $1, 2, 3, 3$ (for example codewords $0, 10, 110, 111$), with
$$E[\ell] = 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.6 + 0.3 = 1.9,$$
while $H(Y) \approx 1.846$. Huffman codes are known to be optimal among prefix codes, so no code does better than $1.9$ bits per symbol here; the entropy is reached only in the limit of long blocks.

blocks.body: Show that any method that sorts $n$ distinct numbers using comparisons needs, on average over the $n!$ equally likely input orders, at least $\log_2 n!$ comparisons. How many does this give for $n = 5$?
blocks.solution:
Run the algorithm and record the outcome of each comparison as a bit. Different input orders must produce different records, since the algorithm must rearrange them differently, and no record is a proper prefix of another: the algorithm's next step depends only on the outcomes seen so far, so if it stopped on one input after a given record, it would stop at the same moment on any input producing the same outcomes. The records therefore form a prefix code for the uniformly random permutation, whose entropy is $\log_2 n!$. By the source coding theorem the expected number of comparisons is at least $\log_2 n!$.

For $n = 5$, $\log_2 120 \approx 6.907$, so the average is at least $6.907$ and in particular the worst case needs at least $7$ comparisons. Seven do suffice for five numbers; the merge-insertion method of Ford and Johnson achieves this. For large $n$, Stirling's formula gives $\log_2 n! = n\log_2 n - n\log_2 e + O(\log n)$, which is why good sorting algorithms run in about $n\log n$ steps.

blocks.body:
Prove that for $0 < k < n$,
$$\binom{n}{k} \le 2^{n h(k/n)},$$
where $h$ is the binary entropy function, and evaluate both sides for $n = 100$, $k = 25$.
blocks.solution:
Let $p = k/n$. By the binomial theorem,
$$1 = \sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n}{j}p^j(1-p)^{n-j} \ge \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.$$
Now $\log_2\left(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\right) = n\left(p\log_2 p + (1-p)\log_2(1-p)\right) = -n\,h(p)$, so the right-hand side is $\binom nk 2^{-nh(p)}$, and rearranging gives the claim.

For $n = 100$, $k = 25$: $h(1/4) \approx 0.8113$, so the bound is $2^{81.13} \approx 2.64 \times 10^{24}$, while $\binom{100}{25} \approx 2.43 \times 10^{23}$. The bound is off by a factor of about $11$, but on the logarithmic scale it is sharp: since the $j = k$ term is the largest of the $n + 1$ terms, it is at least $1/(n+1)$, giving $\binom nk \ge 2^{nh(k/n)}/(n+1)$. So $\log_2\binom{n}{k} = n\,h(k/n) + O(\log n)$, and entropy is the growth rate of binomial coefficients.

blocks.body:
- The base of the logarithm only sets the unit. Mixing bases inside one calculation is a common source of wrong numbers.
- $H(Y \mid X) \le H(Y)$ holds on average, not for each value: learning a particular $x$ can increase uncertainty. For example, let $X = 0$ with probability $3/4$, in which case $Y = 0$, and $X = 1$ with probability $1/4$, in which case $Y$ is a fair bit. Then $H(Y) = h(1/8) \approx 0.544$, but $H(Y \mid X = 1) = 1$. On average $H(Y \mid X) = 1/4$.
- $D(p\,\|\,q) \ne D(q\,\|\,p)$ in general, and $D$ can be infinite.
- For a density $f$, the differential entropy $-\int f\ln f$ behaves differently: it can be negative (uniform on $[0, 1/2]$ gives $-\ln 2$) and changes under rescaling. Relative entropy between densities keeps all the good properties.

Relative entropy is the exponent in large-deviation estimates: the Chernoff bound from [[moment-generating]] functions for a coin with bias $p$ gives $P(\text{at least } an \text{ heads}) \le 2^{-nD(a\,\|\,p)}$ for $a > p$, with $D$ computed between the coins with biases $a$ and $p$. Maximum likelihood in [[point-estimation]] is the same as minimising relative entropy from the empirical distribution, and the log-likelihood ratio statistics of [[hypothesis-testing]] estimate it. The law of large numbers from [[limit-theorems]] applied to $\log_2(1/p(X_i))$ shows that a long random message of $n$ symbols almost surely has probability $2^{-n(H + o(1))}$, which is the heart of Shannon's theorems. In combinatorics, entropy bounds like the binomial one above are a standard tool alongside the [[probabilistic-method]], and the entropy rate of a [[markov-chains|Markov chain]] measures the information produced per step.

1. Compute the entropy of the total of two fair dice, in bits.
2. Show that if $Y = g(X)$ for some function $g$, then $H(Y) \le H(X)$. (Hint: use the chain rule on $H(X, Y)$ in two ways.)
3. Among distributions on $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ with mean $\mu$, show that the geometric distribution $p(k) = (1-r)r^k$ with $r = \mu/(1 + \mu)$ has the largest entropy, by computing $D(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0$ for $q$ geometric.
4. Twelve coins look alike; one is counterfeit and is either heavier or lighter. Use entropy to show that three weighings on a balance (three outcomes each) cannot be beaten in the worst case.

entry.sum: Conditional expectation $E[X \mid \mathcal G]$ is the best prediction of $X$ from the information $\mathcal G$, and a martingale is a sequence with $E[M_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] = M_n$: the fortune in a fair game. Optional stopping, the martingale convergence theorem and the Azuma–Hoeffding inequality turn this one identity into hitting probabilities, almost sure limits and concentration bounds.
entry.why: Martingales compute ruin probabilities and expected waiting times in a few lines, give the general almost sure convergence theorems of probability, and provide the concentration inequalities behind random graph theory, randomised algorithms and the pricing of financial derivatives.

links.note: Azuma's inequality applied to an exposure (Doob) martingale shows that quantities such as the chromatic number of a random graph are concentrated within about $\sqrt n$ of their means.
Martingale concentration bounds analyse randomised algorithms and online learning, where the steps are dependent but each has bounded effect.
Wald's sequential probability ratio test uses the likelihood ratio, a martingale under the null hypothesis, and optional stopping to control its error rates.

refs: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

blocks.body:
A gambler plays a fair game, one unit per round, and has a plan: stop as soon as she is ahead, or double the stake after each loss, or quit when the table looks cold. Can any such plan turn a fair game into a favourable one? Within reasonable limits, no, and martingales explain why and where the limits lie. A martingale models the fortune of a player in a fair game: given everything that has happened so far, the expected fortune after the next round equals the present fortune.

Beyond gambling, martingales give clean computations of hitting probabilities and waiting times, general convergence theorems, and concentration inequalities used throughout combinatorics and computer science. They need one tool first: conditional expectation given a body of information rather than a single event.

blocks.title: Conditioning on information
blocks.body:
From [[joint-distributions]] you know $E[X \mid Y]$ when $Y$ is discrete: on the event $\{Y = y\}$ it equals the average of $X$ over that event, $E[X \mid Y = y]$. So $E[X \mid Y]$ is itself a random variable, a function of $Y$, and it is the best guess of $X$ by someone who knows only $Y$. Two facts characterise it: it is a function of $Y$, and for every event $A$ determined by $Y$, averaging $E[X \mid Y]$ over $A$ gives the same result as averaging $X$ over $A$.

The second description makes sense for any body of information. Information is modelled by a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal G$ of events, the events whose occurrence is known. Knowing $Y$ corresponds to $\mathcal G = \sigma(Y)$, the events of the form $\{Y \in B\}$. A random variable $Z$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable if its value is determined by that information, that is, $\{Z \le z\} \in \mathcal G$ for every $z$.

blocks.title: Conditional expectation
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a random variable with $E|X| < \infty$ and let $\mathcal G$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of the events. A conditional expectation of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ is a random variable $Z = E[X \mid \mathcal G]$ such that

1. $Z$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $E|Z| < \infty$, and
2. $E[Z\,\mathbf 1_A] = E[X\,\mathbf 1_A]$ for every $A \in \mathcal G$.

Such a $Z$ exists and is unique up to events of probability zero (by the Radon–Nikodym theorem, or by orthogonal projection in $L^2$ followed by approximation). It is the $\mathcal G$-measurable random variable that best predicts $X$.

blocks.title: Rules of computation, and filtrations
blocks.body:
The rules used constantly, all consequences of the definition (we omit the proofs, which are in the references; equalities hold with probability $1$):

- Linearity: $E[aX + bY \mid \mathcal G] = aE[X \mid \mathcal G] + bE[Y \mid \mathcal G]$.
- Taking out what is known: if $W$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $WX$ is integrable, $E[WX \mid \mathcal G] = W\,E[X \mid \mathcal G]$.
- Tower property: if $\mathcal H \subseteq \mathcal G$, then $E\big[E[X \mid \mathcal G] \mid \mathcal H\big] = E[X \mid \mathcal H]$. In particular $E\big[E[X \mid \mathcal G]\big] = E[X]$.
- Independence: if $X$ is independent of $\mathcal G$, then $E[X \mid \mathcal G] = E[X]$.
- Jensen: if $\varphi$ is convex and $\varphi(X)$ is integrable, $\varphi\big(E[X \mid \mathcal G]\big) \le E[\varphi(X) \mid \mathcal G]$.

Information accumulating over time is a filtration: $\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal F_0 \subseteq \mathcal F_1 \subseteq \mathcal F_2 \subseteq \cdots$, where $\mathcal F_n$ is what is known at time $n$. A sequence $M_n$ is adapted if each $M_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable.

blocks.title: Martingale
blocks.body:
An adapted sequence $(M_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $E|M_n| < \infty$ for all $n$ is a martingale with respect to $(\mathcal F_n)$ if
$$E[M_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] = M_n \quad \text{for all } n \ge 0.$$
It is a submartingale if $E[M_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] \ge M_n$ (a favourable game) and a supermartingale if $E[M_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] \le M_n$ (an unfavourable one).

By the tower property a martingale has constant mean, $E[M_n] = E[M_0]$, and more generally $E[M_m \mid \mathcal F_n] = M_n$ for all $m \ge n$.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.body:
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent with $P(X_i = 1) = P(X_i = -1) = \tfrac12$, let $S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ be simple random walk, and let $\mathcal F_n$ be generated by $X_1, \dots, X_n$. Then:

1. $S_n$ is a martingale: $E[S_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] = S_n + E[X_{n+1}] = S_n$.
2. $S_n^2 - n$ is a martingale: $$E[(S_n + X_{n+1})^2 \mid \mathcal F_n] = S_n^2 + 2S_n E[X_{n+1}] + 1 = S_n^2 + 1$$.
3. For any real $\theta$, $e^{\theta S_n}/(\cosh\theta)^n$ is a martingale, since $E[e^{\theta X}] = \cosh\theta$.
4. If $Z$ is any integrable random variable, $M_n = E[Z \mid \mathcal F_n]$ is a martingale by the tower property: the best guess of $Z$ revised as information arrives. This is a Doob martingale.
5. Pólya's urn. An urn holds one red and one blue ball. Repeatedly draw a ball at random and return it together with a new ball of the same colour. After $n$ draws there are $n + 2$ balls, $R_n$ of them red, and the red fraction $M_n = R_n/(n+2)$ is a martingale: given $R_n = r$, the next fraction is $(r+1)/(n+3)$ with probability $r/(n+2)$ and $r/(n+3)$ otherwise, which averages to $r/(n+2)$.

A betting strategy is a predictable sequence $H_n$ (the stake for round $n$, decided using $\mathcal F_{n-1}$), and the gambler's fortune is $\sum_{k \le n} H_k(M_k - M_{k-1})$. If the stakes are bounded, this is again a martingale: predictable stakes cannot change the fairness of the game.

blocks.title: Stopping time
blocks.body: A random time $T$ with values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}$ is a stopping time if $\{T = n\} \in \mathcal F_n$ for every $n$: whether to stop at time $n$ is decided from what is known at time $n$, without peeking at the future.

blocks.title: Optional stopping theorem
Proof
blocks.body:
Case 1. Write the stopped value as a telescoping sum,
$$M_T = M_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathbf 1\{T \ge k\}\,(M_k - M_{k-1}).$$
The event $\{T \ge k\}$ is the complement of $\{T \le k-1\}$, so it lies in $\mathcal F_{k-1}$. Taking out what is known,
$$E\big[\mathbf 1\{T \ge k\}(M_k - M_{k-1})\big] = E\big[\mathbf 1\{T \ge k\}\,E[M_k - M_{k-1} \mid \mathcal F_{k-1}]\big] = 0,$$
and summing gives $E[M_T] = E[M_0]$.

Cases 2 and 3. Apply case 1 to the bounded stopping time $T \wedge n$ to get $E[M_{T \wedge n}] = E[M_0]$, and let $n \to \infty$. Since $T < \infty$ almost surely, $M_{T \wedge n} \to M_T$. In case 2 the variables are bounded by $K$; in case 3, $|M_{T \wedge n} - M_0| \le K\,T$ with $E[KT] < \infty$. Either way the dominated convergence theorem gives $E[M_{T \wedge n}] \to E[M_T]$.
Gambler's ruin. Simple random walk starts at $a$, where $0 < a < N$, and stops at the first time $T$ it hits $0$ or $N$. Find the probability that it hits $N$ first, and $E[T]$.
blocks.solution:
First, $T$ is finite with $E[T] < \infty$: from any position, $N$ consecutive up-steps end the game, so in each block of $N$ steps the game ends with probability at least $2^{-N}$, and $P(T > kN) \le (1 - 2^{-N})^k$.

The walk $S_n$ (started at $a$) is a martingale with $|S_{n \wedge T}| \le N$, so case 2 gives $E[S_T] = a$. But $S_T$ is $N$ with some probability $p$ and $0$ otherwise, so $pN = a$ and
$$P(\text{hit } N \text{ before } 0) = \frac aN.$$
For the duration, $S_n^2 - n$ is a martingale. Apply case 1 at $T \wedge n$: $E[S_{T \wedge n}^2] = a^2 + E[T \wedge n]$. As $n \to \infty$ the left side tends to $E[S_T^2]$ (bounded convergence) and the right to $a^2 + E[T]$ (monotone convergence). Since $E[S_T^2] = \frac aN\cdot N^2 = aN$,
$$E[T] = aN - a^2 = a(N - a).$$
For $a = 3$, $N = 10$: the walker reaches $10$ first with probability $0.3$, after $21$ steps on average.

blocks.body: A fair coin is tossed until the pattern HTH appears for the first time. Find the expected number of tosses, and compare with HHH.
blocks.solution:
Before each toss a new gambler arrives with one unit and bets it, at fair odds, that the next toss is H; if she wins (now holding $2$) she bets everything that the following toss is T, and then that the next is H, quitting when she has either lost or completed the pattern. Each bet is fair, so the casino's total profit $M_n$ is a martingale with $M_0 = 0$. Its increments are bounded and $T$, the time HTH is completed, has finite mean (each block of three tosses completes it with probability $1/8$), so case 3 gives $E[M_T] = 0$.

At time $T$ the casino has received $T$ units. It pays out to the gamblers still alive: the one who started at toss $T - 2$ holds $2^3 = 8$; the one who started at toss $T - 1$ lost on T; the one who started at toss $T$ has just won with H and holds $2$. So $M_T = T - 8 - 2$, and $E[T] = 10$.

For HHH every one of the last three gamblers is still winning, holding $8$, $4$ and $2$, so $E[T] = 14$. The general rule: $E[T]$ is the sum of $2^k$ over those $k$ for which the first $k$ letters of the pattern equal its last $k$ letters. Patterns that overlap themselves take longer to appear.

blocks.title: Two pillars: convergence and concentration
blocks.body:
1. (Convergence.) If $(M_n)$ is a submartingale with $\sup_n E|M_n| < \infty$, then $M_n$ converges with probability $1$ to a finite limit $M_\infty$. In particular every nonnegative supermartingale converges almost surely.
2. (Azuma–Hoeffding.) If $(M_n)$ is a martingale with $|M_k - M_{k-1}| \le c_k$ for all $k$, then for every $\lambda > 0$
$$P(M_n - M_0 \ge \lambda) \le \exp\left(-\frac{\lambda^2}{2\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2}\right).$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Part 1 (sketch). Fix $a < b$. Doob's upcrossing inequality, proved by analysing the strategy "buy when the price drops below $a$, sell when it rises above $b$", bounds the expected number of crossings from below $a$ to above $b$ by $E[(M_n - a)^+]/(b - a)$, uniformly in $n$. So with probability $1$ there are only finitely many such crossings, for all rational $a < b$ at once, which rules out oscillation; Fatou's lemma shows the limit is finite.

Part 2 (complete). Let $D_k = M_k - M_{k-1}$, so $E[D_k \mid \mathcal F_{k-1}] = 0$ and $|D_k| \le c_k$. For $t > 0$, convexity of $x \mapsto e^{tx}$ on $[-c_k, c_k]$ gives
$$e^{tx} \le \frac{c_k - x}{2c_k}e^{-tc_k} + \frac{c_k + x}{2c_k}e^{tc_k},$$
so $E[e^{tD_k} \mid \mathcal F_{k-1}] \le \cosh(tc_k) \le e^{t^2c_k^2/2}$, the last step by comparing Taylor series term by term ($(2j)! \ge 2^j j!$). Conditioning repeatedly with the tower property, $E[e^{t(M_n - M_0)}] \le e^{t^2\sum c_k^2/2}$. Markov's inequality gives $P(M_n - M_0 \ge \lambda) \le e^{-t\lambda + t^2\sum c_k^2/2}$, and choosing $t = \lambda/\sum c_k^2$ gives the bound.

blocks.title: What the pillars give
blocks.body:
The red fraction in Pólya's urn is a martingale with values in $[0,1]$, so by part 1 it converges almost surely. But the limit is random. In fact the number of red balls after $n$ draws is uniform on $\{1, 2, \dots, n+1\}$ (a short induction), so the limit fraction is uniform on $[0,1]$. Early luck is self-reinforcing and never washes out.

Azuma's inequality is how martingales prove concentration. For simple random walk ($c_k = 1$), $P(S_{100} \ge 30) \le e^{-900/200} = e^{-4.5} \approx 0.011$; the true value is about $0.0018$. The power lies in Doob martingales: if a quantity $Z$ depends on independent choices $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$ and changing one $Y_k$ changes $Z$ by at most $c_k$, then $M_k = E[Z \mid Y_1, \dots, Y_k]$ has increments bounded by $c_k$, and $Z$ is concentrated within about $\sqrt{\sum c_k^2}$ of its mean. This is how one proves that the chromatic number of a random graph is sharply concentrated, without knowing its value.

- Optional stopping needs a hypothesis. Let simple random walk start at $0$ and stop at the first time $T$ it hits $1$. Then $T < \infty$ almost surely, but $S_T = 1$, so $E[S_T] = 1 \ne 0 = E[S_0]$. Here $E[T] = \infty$ and the walk is unbounded below before $T$, so none of the three cases applies. The doubling strategy fails for the same reason: it needs unlimited credit and unlimited time.
- Almost sure convergence does not imply convergence of means. Let $Y_i$ be independent, equal to $0$ or $2$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each, and $M_n = Y_1\cdots Y_n$. This is a nonnegative martingale with $E[M_n] = 1$, yet $M_n = 0$ for all large $n$ with probability $1$. Convergence in mean needs uniform integrability.

Martingales in continuous time lead straight to [[brownian-motion]], which is the basic continuous martingale; $B_t^2 - t$ and $e^{\theta B_t - \theta^2 t/2}$ play the roles of $S_n^2 - n$ and the exponential martingale, and optional stopping solves the [[heat-equation|heat]] and [[laplace-equation|Laplace]] equations probabilistically. For a [[markov-chains|Markov chain]] and bounded $f$, $f(X_n)$ is a martingale for every starting state exactly when $f$ is harmonic for the transition matrix ($Pf = f$), which links hitting probabilities to linear equations. The strong law in [[limit-theorems]] has a martingale proof, the Radon–Nikodym derivative of [[lebesgue]] theory appears as a martingale limit, and Azuma's inequality is a standard companion of the [[probabilistic-method]].

1. Let each step be $+1$ with probability $p \ne \tfrac12$ and $-1$ with probability $q = 1 - p$. Show that $(q/p)^{S_n}$ is a martingale, deduce that the walk started at $a$ hits $N$ before $0$ with probability $\dfrac{1 - (q/p)^a}{1 - (q/p)^N}$, and use the martingale $S_n - (p - q)n$ to find $E[T]$.

entry.sum: Brownian motion $B_t$ is the scaling limit of a random walk, $S_{\lfloor nt\rfloor}/\sqrt n \to B_t$: a random continuous path with independent increments and $B_t - B_s \sim N(0, t-s)$. Its paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable, with quadratic variation $t$, and its transition density is the heat kernel, so expectations of Brownian motion solve the heat equation.
entry.why: It is the universal limit of random walks (Donsker's theorem), the model for diffusion in physics and for noise in stochastic differential equations and finance, and it gives probabilistic solutions of the heat and Laplace equations.

links.note: Brownian paths give a natural example of continuous functions that are differentiable nowhere and have infinite variation on every interval, yet finite quadratic variation.

The limiting distributions of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov and related goodness-of-fit statistics are functionals of the Brownian bridge, by Donsker's invariance principle for empirical distribution functions.

refs: Karatzas & Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus

blocks.body:
In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown watched tiny particles released from pollen grains jiggle ceaselessly in water. In 1905 Einstein explained the motion as the result of countless collisions with water molecules and predicted that the mean squared displacement grows linearly in time; measurements of this growth by Perrin helped convince physicists that atoms are real. Mathematically, the jiggling particle is the limit of a random walk whose steps become very small and very frequent, and the limit object, Brownian motion, is the most important random process in mathematics.

This page builds Brownian motion from the random walk, shows how wild its paths are, proves the reflection principle and explains the link with the heat equation. It uses the central limit theorem from [[limit-theorems]] and discrete [[martingales]].

blocks.title: Rescaling a random walk
blocks.body:
Let $S_k$ be simple random walk, with independent steps $\pm1$, each with probability $\tfrac12$. After $k$ steps it has mean $0$ and variance $k$, so its typical distance from the start is $\sqrt k$: about $10$ after $100$ steps, about $100$ after $10{,}000$. To see a limit we must shrink space by $\sqrt n$ when we speed up time by $n$. Define
$$W^{(n)}(t) = \frac{S_{\lfloor nt\rfloor}}{\sqrt n}, \qquad t \ge 0.$$
For fixed $t$, the central limit theorem says that $W^{(n)}(t)$ converges in distribution to $N(0, t)$. For $s < t$, the increment $W^{(n)}(t) - W^{(n)}(s)$ is built from steps disjoint from those making up $W^{(n)}(s)$, so in the limit increments over disjoint time intervals are independent normals with variance equal to the length of the interval. Any other scaling, such as dividing by $n$ or by $n^{1/3}$, gives a limit that is identically $0$ or does not exist. The square root is forced.

blocks.title: Brownian motion
Existence and the invariance principle
blocks.body:
1. (Wiener, 1923.) Brownian motion exists. One construction: with $Z_0, Z_1, Z_2, \dots$ independent $N(0,1)$,
$$B_t = Z_0\,t + \sqrt2\sum_{k=1}^\infty Z_k\,\frac{\sin(k\pi t)}{k\pi}, \qquad 0 \le t \le 1,$$
converges uniformly on $[0,1]$ with probability $1$ and defines a Brownian motion on $[0,1]$; independent copies can be glued end to end to cover all $t \ge 0$.
2. (Donsker's invariance principle.) If the steps of the walk are any independent, identically distributed variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$, the linearly interpolated paths $W^{(n)}$ converge in distribution to $B$ as random continuous functions. In particular, $E[\Phi(W^{(n)})] \to E[\Phi(B)]$ for every bounded continuous functional $\Phi$ of paths on $[0,1]$, for example $\Phi(w) = g\big(\max_{t \le 1} w(t)\big)$ with $g$ bounded and continuous. Both parts are stated without proof.

blocks.title: Why the construction works, and why it matters
blocks.body:
The series in part 1 is a [[fourier-series|Fourier sine series]] with random coefficients. It is a Gaussian process, so it is determined by its covariance, and the covariance is right because
$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{2\sin(k\pi s)\sin(k\pi t)}{k^2\pi^2} = \min(s, t) - st \quad (0 \le s, t \le 1),$$
the sine expansion of the "tent" function; adding $Z_0 t$ contributes $st$, giving $\operatorname{Cov}(B_s, B_t) = \min(s,t)$. The proof is completed by checking uniform convergence, which takes real work, and we omit it.

Donsker's theorem is why Brownian motion is universal: whatever the step distribution, a long walk looks Brownian from far away, just as the central limit theorem makes sums look normal. Questions about long walks (the largest excursion, the time spent positive) can therefore be answered by computing once for $B$.

blocks.title: Basic properties
blocks.body:
From the definition, directly:

- Covariance: for $s \le t$, $E[B_sB_t] = E[B_s^2] + E[B_s(B_t - B_s)] = s$. So $\operatorname{Cov}(B_s, B_t) = \min(s, t)$.
- Scaling: for $c > 0$, $c^{-1/2}B_{ct}$ is again a standard Brownian motion. Zooming in by a factor $c$ in time and $\sqrt c$ in space gives the same picture, so the paths are statistically self-similar.
- Symmetry and time inversion: $-B_t$ is a Brownian motion, and so is $tB_{1/t}$ (set to $0$ at $t = 0$).
- Markov property: for fixed $s$, $(B_{s+t} - B_s)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Brownian motion independent of $(B_u)_{u \le s}$. The strong Markov property (stated here without proof) says the same holds when $s$ is replaced by a stopping time such as the first time $B$ hits a level.
- Martingales: with $\mathcal F_s$ the information in $(B_u)_{u \le s}$, the processes $B_t$, $B_t^2 - t$ and $e^{\theta B_t - \theta^2 t/2}$ are martingales, by the same calculation as for $S_n$, $S_n^2 - n$ and the exponential martingale of the random walk.

blocks.title: Quadratic variation
blocks.body:
For $t > 0$ and partitions $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = t$ with mesh $\max_k(t_k - t_{k-1}) \to 0$,
$$Q_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \left(B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}}\right)^2 \longrightarrow t \quad \text{in mean square}.$$
Consequently, with probability $1$ the path has infinite total variation on every interval. In fact (Paley, Wiener and Zygmund) with probability $1$ the path is differentiable at no point.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $\Delta_k = t_k - t_{k-1}$. The increments are independent with $(B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}})^2 = \Delta_k Z_k^2$, where $Z_k \sim N(0,1)$. Since $E[Z^2] = 1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z^2) = 2$,
$$E[Q_n] = \sum \Delta_k = t, \qquad E\left[(Q_n - t)^2\right] = \operatorname{Var}(Q_n) = 2\sum_k \Delta_k^2 \le 2t\max_k\Delta_k \to 0.$$
For the consequence, $Q_n \le \max_k|B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}}|\cdot\sum_k|B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}}|$. Pass to a subsequence of partitions along which $Q_n \to t > 0$ almost surely. The maximum tends to $0$ by uniform continuity of the path on $[0,t]$, so the sum, which is at most the total variation, must tend to infinity. The same argument on each of the countably many intervals with rational endpoints (the increments of $B$ over $[r, r']$ form a Brownian motion run for time $r' - r$) gives infinite variation on all of them at once with probability $1$, hence on every interval. The nowhere-differentiability theorem needs a finer argument, which we omit.

blocks.title: Rough paths and a new calculus
blocks.body:
For a smooth function, the sum of squared increments over a fine partition tends to $0$; for Brownian motion it tends to $t$. Heuristically $(dB)^2 = dt$: over a time $\Delta$ the path moves about $\sqrt\Delta$, which is much larger than $\Delta$, so the slope $\Delta B/\Delta$ is of size $\Delta^{-1/2}$ and blows up. This is why calculus with Brownian motion needs new rules. In Itô's calculus, the extra term from $(dB)^2 = dt$ gives
$$\int_0^t B_s\,dB_s = \tfrac12\left(B_t^2 - t\right),$$
not the $\tfrac12 B_t^2$ that ordinary calculus would suggest; notice that the right side is the martingale $\tfrac12(B_t^2 - t)$.

blocks.title: Reflection principle
blocks.body:
For $a > 0$ and $t > 0$,
$$P\left(\max_{0 \le s \le t} B_s \ge a\right) = 2P(B_t \ge a) = 2\left(1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt t}\right)\right),$$
where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. Equivalently, $\max_{s \le t}B_s$ has the same distribution as $|B_t|$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $T_a$ be the first time $B$ reaches $a$; then $\max_{s \le t}B_s \ge a$ exactly when $T_a \le t$. On this event, by the strong Markov property, the path after $T_a$ is a Brownian motion started at $a$, independent of the past, and so is its mirror image in the level $a$. Reflecting the part after $T_a$ therefore maps Brownian paths with $T_a \le t$ to Brownian paths with $T_a \le t$ and preserves probability; it exchanges paths ending above $a$ with paths ending below $a$. Hence
$$P(T_a \le t,\ B_t < a) = P(T_a \le t,\ B_t > a) = P(B_t > a),$$
the last step because $B_t > a$ forces $T_a \le t$ by continuity. Adding $P(T_a \le t, B_t \ge a) = P(B_t \ge a)$ and using $P(B_t = a) = 0$ gives the result.

For simple random walk the same argument is an exact bijection of paths: for integers $a \ge 1$, $P(\max_{k \le n}S_k \ge a) = P(S_n \ge a) + P(S_n > a)$.

blocks.title: Brownian motion and the heat equation
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be bounded and continuous and set $u(t, x) = E[f(x + B_t)]$, the expected value of $f$ at the position of a Brownian particle started at $x$. Since $x + B_t \sim N(x, t)$,
$$u(t, x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(y)\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}e^{-(y - x)^2/(2t)}\,dy,$$
and differentiating the kernel shows that
$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \frac12\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}, \qquad u(0, x) = f(x).$$
The transition density of Brownian motion is the heat kernel: the density of a cloud of Brownian particles spreads exactly as heat does, which is the content of Einstein's analysis. In several dimensions the same holds with the Laplacian, and the probability that Brownian motion started at $x$ leaves a region through a given part of the boundary is a harmonic function of $x$; this solves the Dirichlet problem for the [[laplace-equation]].
Find the distribution of $B_1 + B_2$, and compute $P(B_1 > 0,\ B_2 > 0)$.
blocks.solution:
$B_1 + B_2 = 2B_1 + (B_2 - B_1)$ is a sum of independent normals, with variance $4\cdot1 + 1 = 5$, so $B_1 + B_2 \sim N(0, 5)$.

For the probability, condition on $B_1 = x > 0$: then $B_2 = x + (B_2 - B_1)$ with an independent $N(0,1)$ increment, so $P(B_2 > 0 \mid B_1 = x) = \Phi(x)$. Hence
$$P(B_1 > 0, B_2 > 0) = \int_0^\infty \Phi(x)\varphi(x)\,dx = \left[\tfrac12\Phi(x)^2\right]_0^\infty = \tfrac12\left(1 - \tfrac14\right) = \tfrac38.$$
Positive correlation between $B_1$ and $B_2$ makes this larger than the $\tfrac14$ we would get for independent variables.

blocks.body: Find the probability that a standard Brownian motion exceeds $1$ at some time before $t = 1$, and show that the first hitting time $T_a$ of a level $a > 0$ is finite with probability $1$ but has infinite mean.
blocks.solution:
By the reflection principle, $P(\max_{s \le 1}B_s \ge 1) = 2(1 - \Phi(1)) \approx 0.3173$.

More generally $P(T_a \le t) = 2(1 - \Phi(a/\sqrt t))$, which tends to $2(1 - \Phi(0)) = 1$ as $t \to \infty$, so $T_a < \infty$ almost surely. For large $t$,
$$P(T_a > t) = 2\Phi\!\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt t}\right) - 1 = 2\int_0^{a/\sqrt t}\varphi(z)\,dz \ge \frac{2a}{\sqrt t}\,\varphi(a) \quad (t \ge 1),$$
using $\varphi(z) \ge \varphi(a)$ on $[0, a/\sqrt t] \subseteq [0, a]$. Since $\int_1^\infty t^{-1/2}\,dt = \infty$, $E[T_a] = \int_0^\infty P(T_a > t)\,dt = \infty$. The Brownian particle will certainly reach $a$, but on average it takes forever, exactly like the simple random walk waiting to reach $1$.

blocks.body: Let $a, b > 0$ and let $\tau$ be the first time $B$ leaves the interval $(-a, b)$. Find $P(B_\tau = b)$ and $E[\tau]$.
blocks.solution:
This is gambler's ruin in continuous time, and the optional stopping theorem holds for Brownian martingales under the same kind of conditions as in discrete time (a fact we use without proof). $B_{t \wedge \tau}$ is bounded by $\max(a, b)$, and $\tau < \infty$ almost surely (it is at most $T_b$), so $E[B_\tau] = 0$. If $p = P(B_\tau = b)$, then $pb - (1 - p)a = 0$ and
$$P(B_\tau = b) = \frac{a}{a + b}.$$
Next, $B_t^2 - t$ is a martingale, so $E[B_{t \wedge \tau}^2] = E[t \wedge \tau]$. Letting $t \to \infty$ (bounded convergence on the left, monotone convergence on the right),
$$E[\tau] = E[B_\tau^2] = \frac{a}{a+b}\,b^2 + \frac{b}{a+b}\,a^2 = ab.$$
Compare the random walk answer $a(N - a)$ for the walk started at $a$ in $[0, N]$: it is the same formula after shifting the start to $0$.

blocks.body:
- Displacement grows like $\sqrt t$, not like $t$. Doubling the time multiplies the typical distance by $\sqrt2$.
- $dB_t/dt$ does not exist, so equations "with white noise" need Itô's calculus; the ordinary chain rule fails, as $\int_0^t B\,dB = \tfrac12(B_t^2 - t)$ shows.
- Properties 1 to 3 of the definition do not by themselves give continuous paths; continuity is a separate requirement, and existence of a process with all four properties is a theorem.
- Optional stopping needs conditions here too: $E[B_{T_1}] = 1 \ne 0$ although $B$ is a martingale, because $T_1$ has infinite mean and $B$ is unbounded below before $T_1$.
- In the discrete reflection principle the boundary term matters: $P(\max S_k \ge a) = P(S_n \ge a) + P(S_n > a)$, not $2P(S_n \ge a)$.

Brownian motion is the continuous-time [[martingales|martingale]] par excellence and the scaling limit of the random walks of [[markov-chains]] and [[limit-theorems]]. Its transition density is the kernel of the [[heat-equation]], and exit distributions solve the Dirichlet problem for the [[laplace-equation]]; in two dimensions, Brownian paths are invariant under [[conformal-maps]] up to a time change, which gives probabilistic proofs of results in complex analysis. Simulating Brownian paths by [[monte-carlo]] is the standard way to evaluate expectations in stochastic models, including option prices in the Black–Scholes model, where a stock price is $S_0e^{\sigma B_t + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)t}$. The Fourier-series construction connects it with [[fourier-series]] and [[hilbert-spaces]] (an orthonormal expansion with independent Gaussian coefficients).

1. Show that $X_t = tB_{1/t}$ (with $X_0 = 0$) has the covariance $\min(s,t)$ of Brownian motion.
2. Show that $P(B_s > 0 \text{ for all } s \in (0, \varepsilon]) = 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$. (Hint: use scaling and the reflection principle on $-B$.)
3. Use the exponential martingale with $\theta = \sqrt{2\lambda}$ and optional stopping to show $E[e^{-\lambda T_a}] = e^{-a\sqrt{2\lambda}}$ for $\lambda > 0$.
4. For simple random walk, verify the discrete reflection identity $P(\max_{k \le 4}S_k \ge 2) = P(S_4 \ge 2) + P(S_4 > 2)$ by listing paths.
